solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

definitions.meaning: lying on one's front, the face to the floor
to stare someone out or defy them openly

explanation.surface: Inclined to take people on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prone to' reads as 'inclined to'; split it into 'prone' (lying flat) and 'confront'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: lying flat with the face to the floor, and the idiom for defying an opponent head-on.

clue.text: Protection for top Liberal theme following review?

indicators.note: after a review the letters are revised into a new order

explanation.surface: A political party's leading idea is reconsidered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like a party leader; it is the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: protective headgear, guarding the top of the body, i.e. the head.

clue.text: Bishop, one putting on fat in time

indicators.note: the fat is put on around the bishop and one, as a garment is put on

parts.note: podge is excess fat
RR, Right Reverend, is the title of a bishop
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A cleric gaining weight over the years.
explanation.walkthrough: British slang: 'doing porridge' means serving a prison sentence, i.e. doing time.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a prison sentence, as in serving time, hence the 1970s sitcom set in a jail.

clue.text: Hutchinson, exposed endlessly, with no time to absorb shock?

indicators.note: exposed, as in shown up and laid open, signals the letters are rearranged; the setter admitted the indicator was disputed
with no means a letter is taken away
endlessly means the name loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone called Hutchinson, caught out and short of time, must ride out the blow.
explanation.walkthrough: Strip H and N from HUTCHINSON, then the first T, leaving UCHINSO for 'exposed' to rearrange; Monk said he had first used 'cruelly' as the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb sense: to soften or deaden the impact of something, as padding does.

parts.note: an angle is a corner

explanation.surface: A magistrate's corner of the room has been disturbed.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb sense: to jar or set on edge, as in nerves that are frayed and disturbed.

parts.note: full means complete, perfect
to stay is to stop

explanation.surface: Finish an ideal visit.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom and punctuation: the dot ending a sentence, also used for a complete halt.

clue.text: Put down hollow dome on base

indicators.note: hollow means emptied, so only the outside letters remain

parts.note: base and mean both mean low or ignoble

explanation.surface: Lower an empty cupola onto its foundation.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to degrade or belittle someone, lowering their dignity.

clue.text: In the main, stopped censor stifling setter

definitions.note: at sea (the main), a ship that comes to has halted

indicators.note: the censor's name smothers the setter's word, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Cato the Elder was the famous Roman censor
the setter refers to himself as me

explanation.surface: A sailor's tale of a voyage halted when the official silenced the puzzle compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is the old word for the open sea, where a vessel 'comes to' when it stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Nautical idiom: a vessel that heaves to and halts is said to come to, so stopped at sea fits.

parts.note: Una is a girl's name
to muse is to meditate, so meditated gives mused

explanation.surface: A girl sat in quiet contemplation, as solemn as the old Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Victoria is famously credited with the line 'We are not amused'.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: the remark attributed to Queen Victoria, 'We are not amused', makes her the type of someone unentertained.

indicators.note: the remaining letters are treated terribly, i.e. jumbled into a new order
losing the heart means the central letter of cherubims goes

explanation.surface: Angels painted without feeling and rendered dreadfully lifeless.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the middle U from CHERUBIMS leaves CHERBIMS, which 'terribly' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Verb sense: to dull a surface or reputation is to tarnish or sully it, which is what smearing does.

indicators.note: desperately suggests wild disorder, so the letters of longed are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone yearned wildly to find contentment.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the sense of blissful, as in the happy, prosperous days of one's youth.

clue.text: Smelly opponent almost put in order

parts.note: a foe is an opponent

indicators.note: almost means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to tidy is to put in order

explanation.surface: A malodorous rival is nearly organised.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something stinking or rank has a foul smell.

indicators.note: following places the word for individual after the word for public

parts.note: overt means open, done in public
one means a single individual

explanation.surface: A lone person trails behind a public society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Association' looks like a club, but here it means a suggestion or connotation.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the sense of connotation: an implied meaning or suggestion carried alongside the literal one.

clue.text: Critic of queen going on strike

indicators.note: going on means the queen's letters are attached after the strike word

parts.note: to knock is to strike
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the queen

explanation.surface: A commentator on the monarch joining industrial action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' reads as a walkout, but it means a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal synonym: someone who constantly disparages or finds fault, from 'knock' meaning to criticise.

clue.text: It's a doddle to harden pace

parts.note: to cake is to harden into a crust
a walk is a pace

explanation.surface: Setting hard and walking briskly is no trouble at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doddle' is British slang for a very easy task.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: something absurdly easy, from the old prize dance where competitors won a cake.

clue.text: Home secretary ringing operator by means of receivers?

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so the cabinet minister's letters surround the rest

parts.note: HS is the abbreviation for Home Secretary
per means by means of, as in 'per post'

explanation.surface: A government minister phoning a switchboard via handsets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringing' and 'receivers' suggest telephones; a hopper is a funnel-shaped container that receives grain or coal.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a hopper is a container into which material is fed, hence a receiver; the question mark marks the loose fit.

parts.note: reads as a brief glance, but describes the announcement of a death, a passing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Passing' looks like 'casual'; it is a euphemism for death.
explanation.definitionFit: Euphemism: a death is a passing, and the newspaper piece marking it is that notice.

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are made anew in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A story taken from an Eastern work of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book; it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the telling or recounting of a story is a narrative account.

parts.note: a toad is a contemptible person, a creep

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means reading upwards, so the letters are turned back

parts.note: re means on, concerning

explanation.surface: An amphibian clambering onto a shrub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toad' is the insult for a nasty person, not the amphibian.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a vine or ivy that trails along the ground or climbs walls is this kind of plant.

indicators.note: these words say the answer is to be read as an order whose result is the crucifix, a command to turn a word round

parts.note: a crucifix is a rood, which is what the word door spells when turned back

explanation.surface: A cryptic order hidden in a religious cross.
explanation.walkthrough: ROOD is an old word for a crucifix; read the answer as a command, 'back' (reverse) 'door', to get it.
explanation.definitionFit: Adjectival sense: something underhand or clandestine, like a deal made by an unofficial route, is secret.

parts.note: an ad is an announcement, an advertisement
here means beside the speaker, by me

explanation.surface: Consenting to a statement made by the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym with a following preposition: to stick to or follow a rule, i.e. to go along with it.

indicators.note: endlessly means the first and last letters of moan are removed, leaving its centre

parts.note: rage is anger

explanation.surface: A rower complains bitterly and furiously without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowing' suggests a quarrel; it is the rare word for the action of using oars.
explanation.definitionFit: Archaic noun for the use of oars, the act of propelling a boat by oar.

clue.text: Nearly pierce heart of giant animal

indicators.note: nearly means the last letter is cut

parts.note: to impale is to pierce

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its central letter

explanation.surface: A near miss at skewering a huge beast.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: an African antelope, a familiar grazing animal of the savannah.

clue.text: Fringe of 2 that's soft, not hard

indicators.note: soft, not hard says one letter is swapped for the other

parts.note: the number refers to the solution of 2-down, the protective headgear
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils
P, piano, is the musical abbreviation for soft

explanation.surface: An edging on the headgear that is pliable rather than rigid.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the answer to 2 down and replace its H with P.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a valance or narrow border hiding a curtain rail, a decorative fringe over the window.

definitions.meaning: British slang for a hopeless, incompetent bunch, as in 'what a lot'

explanation.surface: Good-for-nothings take a tumble.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls an inept group a shower, while the everyday sense is a brief fall of rain.

parts.note: quality means character, as in a person of quality

explanation.surface: The English temperament shows a sense of justice.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: fair treatment means everyone stands on the same footing, with no one favoured.

clue.text: Start to play old record when Prudence is around

indicators.note: the nickname is around the other pieces, so they sit inside it

parts.note: Prue is a short form of the name Prudence
a log is a record, as in a ship's log

explanation.surface: A woman named Prudence spins a vintage disc.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre term: the introductory speech or section that opens a drama is its beginning.

clue.text: Might one shout "shoo!" for this beast?

definitions.text: Might one shout "shoo!" for this beast?

parts.words: Might one shout "shoo!" for this beast?
parts.note: the creature is an antelope that might be shooed away, but its name is also a sports-shoe brand, and 'shoo' sounds like 'shoe'

explanation.surface: A farmer wonders whether yelling will scare off some wild animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The beast is a South African antelope whose name is also a famous trainer brand, so 'shoo!' doubles as 'shoe'.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a small grey South African antelope, a beast that also lends its name to a sportswear label.
